“A 28-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks is undergoing CTG monitoring. Interpret the trace and advise on management.”
“A woman in labour has recurrent fetal heart rate decelerations. Assess the CTG and discuss the next steps.”
“Identify the abnormalities on this CTG and explain their clinical significance.”
“A CTG shows a fetal heart rate of 170 beats/min with reduced variability. What is your interpretation and management?”

blocks.title: Cardiotocography is a method of simultaneously recording:

items.text: Fetal heart rate (FHR): usually the upper trace.
Uterine activity: usually the lower trace, showing the timing and approximate frequency of contractions.

blocks.text: It helps assess fetal well-being, particularly during labour, by evaluating the fetal heart rate pattern in relation to uterine contractions.
CTG is not a standalone diagnostic test for fetal hypoxia. Findings must be interpreted alongside the maternal condition, gestational age, stage of labour, medications and the clinical circumstances.
If the station involves a clinical scenario rather than an image alone, begin by stating that you would:

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain CTG monitoring and obtain consent.
Establish the gestational age and whether she is in labour.
Ask about fetal movements, vaginal bleeding, liquor drainage and abdominal pain.
Review relevant risk factors, including previous caesarean section, hypertension, diabetes, fetal growth restriction and meconium-stained liquor.
Assess the mother's observations and general clinical condition.
Confirm that the CTG trace is correctly labelled and that the recorded rate is fetal rather than maternal.

blocks.text: Safety point: If the trace suggests acute fetal compromise, summon senior obstetric help and begin appropriate assessment and resuscitative measures immediately. Do not delay urgent care to complete a lengthy history.

blocks.text: NICE recommends assessing contractions, baseline, variability and decelerations to classify an intrapartum CTG, while also considering accelerations and the whole clinical picture.
NICE

content_groups.group_title: Step 1: Check the trace and clinical context

items.text: Patient's name and identification details.
Gestational age.
Whether the trace is antenatal or intrapartum.
Date and time of recording.
Duration and quality of the trace.
Maternal pulse and whether it could be mistaken for the fetal heart rate.
Relevant clinical history, medications and previous CTG changes.

blocks.text: Important OSCE distinction: NICE's intrapartum CTG classification system should not automatically be applied to antenatal CTGs. Antenatal traces require interpretation according to the relevant antenatal monitoring protocol.
NICE
medical.uworld.com
Assess the frequency, duration and spacing of contractions, and whether the uterus relaxes between them.

rows: Excessive frequency; concerning for reduced recovery time

blocks.text: NICE classifies 5 or more contractions in 10 minutes, or hypertonus, as an amber feature in its intrapartum system.
NICE
Clinical significance: Excessive uterine activity, particularly with oxytocin infusion, can reduce uteroplacental blood flow and contribute to fetal hypoxia.
What to say in the OSCE:
“There are approximately four contractions in 10 minutes, with adequate relaxation between contractions and no evidence of uterine hypertonus.”
Or, if abnormal:

“There are six contractions in 10 minutes, consistent with excessive uterine activity. I would review any uterotonic medication, assess the fetal heart rate and maternal condition, and initiate appropriate measures.”

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Assess the baseline fetal heart rate

blocks.text: The baseline is the average fetal heart rate over a 10-minute period, excluding accelerations and decelerations.
Usual normal baseline in labour
Potentially concerning; a stable baseline with normal variability and no decelerations may be acceptable after clinical assessment.
Red feature in the NICE intrapartum classification system.
NICE
**Causes of an abnormal baseline**
A. Fetal tachycardia: above 160 beats/min

items.text: Maternal fever or intra-amniotic infection.
Maternal dehydration.
Maternal anxiety or pain, sometimes contributing to an increased rate.
Fetal hypoxia.
Maternal medications, including beta-agonists.
Fetal tachyarrhythmia.

blocks.text: B. Fetal bradycardia: below 110 beats/min
A rate between 100 and 109 may sometimes be acceptable if stable and accompanied by normal variability and no decelerations. A rate below 100 is more concerning in the NICE intrapartum system.

items.text: Fetal hypoxia.
Umbilical cord compression or prolapse.
Placental abruption.
Uterine rupture.
Maternal hypotension.
Excessive uterine activity.
Fetal conduction abnormalities or other arrhythmias.

blocks.text: Exam tip: A sudden drop in fetal heart rate is more urgent than a mildly abnormal but stable baseline. Always assess the rate's trend, associated variability and decelerations, and the clinical context.
**Step 4: Assess baseline variability**
Variability is the normal fluctuation in fetal heart rate around the baseline, caused largely by the interaction of the fetal autonomic nervous system and other physiological influences.

rows: Increased variability; assess duration and accompanying features
Very concerning, particularly with decelerations or abnormal baseline

blocks.text: In the NICE intrapartum framework, variability below 5 beats/min for 30–50 minutes is amber, while below 5 for more than 50 minutes is red. Variability above 25 is amber for up to 10 minutes and red when it persists beyond 10 minutes. A sinusoidal pattern is also a red feature.
NICE
**Causes of reduced variability**

items.text: Fetal sleep cycle.
Opioid or sedative medication.
Prematurity.
Fetal hypoxia or acidosis.
Neurological abnormalities.

blocks.text: A short period of reduced variability may be physiological. However, prolonged reduction, especially with a rising baseline or recurrent decelerations, is concerning.
**Increased variability**
Marked variability may be associated with transient fetal stress or evolving compromise, particularly when sustained or accompanied by decelerations.
**Sinusoidal pattern**
A smooth, regular, wave-like pattern with absent normal variability and no ordinary accelerations is highly concerning in the appropriate clinical setting.
Consider severe fetal anaemia, including fetomaternal haemorrhage or red-cell alloimmunisation, among the differential diagnoses.
OSCE phrase:
“Baseline variability is approximately 10 beats per minute, which is within the normal range.”
Or:
“There is persistently reduced baseline variability, which raises concern for fetal compromise, particularly in the presence of recurrent decelerations.”
**Step 5: Assess accelerations**
An acceleration is a transient rise in fetal heart rate of at least 15 beats/min above baseline, lasting at least 15 seconds, in the usual term intrapartum assessment.
stepwards.com
Accelerations are generally reassuring because they indicate fetal responsiveness.

items.text: Accelerations may occur with fetal movement.
Their presence is generally reassuring, even when some variability is reduced.
Their absence on an otherwise normal intrapartum trace does not, by itself, establish fetal acidosis.

blocks.text: NICE
OSCE phrase:
“There are two clear accelerations of at least 15 beats per minute lasting at least 15 seconds, which is a reassuring feature.”
Do not make the mistake of diagnosing fetal distress solely because accelerations are absent.
**Step 6: Assess decelerations**
A deceleration is a transient fall in fetal heart rate. In the usual definition, the rate falls by more than 15 beats/min for at least 15 seconds.
The key is to identify the deceleration's timing, depth, duration, recovery and relationship to contractions.
**A. Early decelerations**
Usually benign
The fetal heart rate gradually falls and recovers in a pattern that mirrors the uterine contraction.
Mechanism: Fetal head compression.
Management: If isolated, with otherwise reassuring features, continue appropriate monitoring and routine care.
**B. Variable decelerations**
Assess severity
Abrupt drops in fetal heart rate with variable timing in relation to contractions. They may be V-, U- or W-shaped.
Mechanism: Usually umbilical cord compression.
Concerning features: Duration over 60 seconds, reduced variability within the deceleration, slow or incomplete recovery, or loss of previously present shouldering.
Management: Review the clinical context, change maternal position if appropriate and obtain urgent review if persistent or accompanied by other abnormalities.
**C. Late decelerations**
Concerning
The fetal heart rate begins to fall after the contraction has started, reaches its lowest point after the contraction's peak, and recovers after the contraction ends.
Mechanism: May reflect uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia.
Management: Urgent obstetric review, correction of reversible causes and consideration of expedited birth according to the overall clinical picture.
**D. Prolonged deceleration**
Obstetric emergency if persistent
A sustained fall in fetal heart rate. A deceleration lasting 3 minutes or longer is a red feature in the NICE intrapartum classification.
Possible causes: Cord prolapse, placental abruption, uterine rupture, maternal hypotension, or excessive uterine activity.
Management: Call for urgent help, assess for an acute obstetric event, start appropriate corrective measures and prepare for urgent birth.
The descriptions and risk criteria above follow NICE intrapartum guidance.
NICE

items.text: Early = head
Variable = cord
Late = placenta
Prolonged = investigate immediately

blocks.text: These are useful associations, not absolute diagnostic rules. A normal-looking pattern does not exclude every cause of fetal compromise, and variable decelerations can be benign when uncomplicated.
For intrapartum CTG interpretation using the NICE system, each of four features is assessed: contractions, baseline, variability and decelerations.
Normal CTG
All four features are white, with no amber or red features.
Suspicious CTG
One amber feature, with no red features.
Pathological CTG
At least one red feature, or at least two amber features.
NICE

Some institutions use other CTG classification systems, including three-tier systems with different definitions. In an OSCE, state which framework you are applying and follow the protocol specified by the examination or institution.

A pathological CTG does not automatically mean that caesarean section is the only possible intervention. The urgency and mode of birth depend on the cause, the stage of labour, cervical dilatation, fetal station, maternal condition and how quickly safe vaginal birth can be achieved.
The central principle is to treat reversible causes promptly, reassess the CTG, and expedite birth when fetal compromise persists or an acute emergency is suspected.

blocks.text: Do not give maternal oxygen routinely solely to treat an abnormal CTG when the mother is not hypoxic. Give oxygen if indicated for maternal hypoxaemia or another maternal clinical indication.

NICE recommends urgent review and preparation for urgent birth for acute bradycardia or a prolonged deceleration lasting at least 3 minutes. If the bradycardia persists, birth should be expedited according to the guideline's time thresholds and clinical circumstances.
NICE

blocks.title: Consider expedited birth when there is:

items.text: Persistent pathological CTG despite appropriate corrective measures.
Acute bradycardia or a prolonged deceleration that does not recover.
Suspected cord prolapse, uterine rupture or significant placental abruption.
Evidence of evolving fetal compromise in the context of additional risk factors.

blocks.text: The route may be operative vaginal birth if all prerequisites are met and it can be achieved safely and promptly, or emergency caesarean section when indicated.
Do not delay an indicated urgent birth while waiting for every possible investigation or intervention.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to report a CTG in the OSCE

blocks.text: Use this structure: Identification → Contractions → Baseline → Variability → Decelerations → Accelerations → Classification → Plan.

“This is an intrapartum CTG of adequate quality. There are four uterine contractions in 10 minutes with adequate relaxation between contractions. The baseline fetal heart rate is approximately 140 beats per minute. Baseline variability is normal at approximately 10 beats per minute. There are no pathological decelerations, and accelerations are present. All four classification features are reassuring, making this a normal CTG under the NICE intrapartum classification system. I would continue appropriate monitoring and regular clinical reassessment.”

content_groups.group_title: Example 2: Fetal tachycardia with reduced variability

blocks.text: “The baseline fetal heart rate is approximately 175 beats per minute, with reduced variability and no clear accelerations. These findings are concerning for possible fetal compromise. I would assess the maternal temperature and observations, investigate possible infection or other reversible causes, review the uterine activity and medications, and obtain urgent senior obstetric review. The need for expedited birth would depend on the full clinical picture and response to initial measures.”

“The baseline fetal heart rate is approximately 150 beats per minute. Recurrent late decelerations are present in relation to uterine contractions. This is a concerning feature suggestive of possible uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia. I would summon urgent obstetric assistance, assess for reversible causes, initiate appropriate corrective measures and consider expedited birth if the abnormal pattern persists or the clinical circumstances demand it.”

“There is an acute, sustained fall in the fetal heart rate from a baseline of 140 beats per minute to approximately 70 beats per minute. This is an obstetric emergency until the cause is established. I would call for immediate assistance, assess the maternal condition and uterine activity, exclude cord prolapse and other acute obstetric events, initiate appropriate corrective measures and prepare for urgent birth if the bradycardia persists.”

blocks.text: These are differential diagnoses, not conclusions from the trace alone.
CTG interpretation is primarily a clinical assessment. Additional investigations depend on the abnormality and the urgency of the situation.

items.text: Maternal observations: Temperature, pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and hydration status.
Bedside assessment: Palpate uterine activity and confirm that the recorded rate is fetal rather than maternal.
Blood tests: Full blood count, inflammatory markers, cultures or other tests when infection or another maternal condition is suspected.
Ultrasound: Useful in selected situations to assess fetal viability, presentation, amniotic fluid or other antenatal concerns.
Fetal blood sampling: May be considered only in selected settings where available, appropriate and safe under local protocols; it must not delay urgent delivery when indicated.

blocks.text: Fetal surveillance • Labour ward emergencies • CTG reporting • Clinical decision-making

Cardiotocography (CTG) is used to assess the fetal heart rate (FHR) and uterine contractions. In an OSCE, you may be asked to interpret a CTG trace, classify it, identify the likely cause of an abnormality and explain the immediate management.
The key principle: Interpret the trace in the clinical context. A CTG is not a diagnosis by itself, and a concerning trace must prompt timely clinical assessment.
You are asked to review a CTG for a woman in labour at 39 weeks' gestation.

blocks.title: The examiner may ask you to:

items.text: Confirm the patient and the indication for CTG.
Identify the baseline fetal heart rate.
Assess baseline variability.
Identify accelerations and decelerations.
Assess uterine contraction frequency and duration.
Classify the CTG using the system specified by the examination.
State your interpretation and management plan.

blocks.text: Other scenarios include fetal bradycardia after an epidural, recurrent late decelerations, variable decelerations after membrane rupture, uterine tachysystole during oxytocin infusion or a prolonged deceleration.
CTG records two main parameters:
Upper trace — fetal heart rate
Shows the fetal heart rate in beats per minute (bpm), including its baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations.
Lower trace — uterine activity
Shows the timing and relative pattern of contractions. An external tocodynamometer does not reliably measure the absolute strength of contractions.
CTG may be used antenatally or during labour. Interpretation depends on the indication, gestational age, maternal condition, labour progress and any relevant medications.

blocks.text: Common OSCE trap: An external monitor may record the maternal pulse instead of the fetal heart rate. If the rate seems inconsistent with the clinical picture, check the maternal pulse and confirm the fetal signal using appropriate methods.

The baseline is the average fetal heart rate over a 10-minute period, excluding accelerations, decelerations and periods of marked variability. There should generally be at least 2 minutes of identifiable baseline within that period; otherwise, the baseline may be described as indeterminate.
Typical baseline
Normal range
Bradycardia
Tachycardia

**A. Normal baseline**
A baseline of 140 bpm with normal variability and no concerning decelerations is generally reassuring.
**B. Fetal bradycardia**

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: Do not diagnose fetal hypoxia from tachycardia alone. Assess variability, decelerations, contractions and the mother's clinical condition.
Variability refers to the small fluctuations around the baseline fetal heart rate. It reflects the interaction between the fetal autonomic nervous system and the heart.

items.text: Normal/moderate variability: approximately 5–25 bpm.
Reduced variability: less than 5 bpm.

Absent variability means that fluctuations are not detectable. When associated with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations or bradycardia, this is a particularly concerning pattern.
Do not confuse reduced variability with a technically poor signal. First ensure that the trace is interpretable.
An acceleration is a transient increase in fetal heart rate above the baseline.
A commonly used definition after 32 weeks' gestation is an increase of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds but less than 10 minutes.
Before 32 weeks, a 10 bpm increase lasting 10 seconds may be used.
Accelerations are generally reassuring because they are commonly associated with an intact fetal autonomic response.

blocks.text: Classification terminology varies by guideline. For an OSCE, state which system you are using and apply it consistently.
Category I — Normal
Reassuring

items.text: Baseline 110–160 bpm.
Moderate variability.
No late or variable decelerations.

blocks.text: Action: Continue appropriate monitoring and routine care if the clinical situation remains reassuring.
Category II — Indeterminate
Requires assessment
Includes traces that are neither clearly normal nor clearly abnormal.
Examples include some cases of tachycardia, reduced variability, or variable decelerations with otherwise reassuring features.
Action: Review the whole trace, reassess the mother, identify reversible causes, increase vigilance and seek senior input when indicated.
Category III — Abnormal
Urgent response
Under the commonly used NICHD/ACOG system, this includes absent variability accompanied by recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern.
Action: Urgent assessment, correction of reversible causes and expedited birth if the pattern does not resolve or the clinical situation demands it.

Important distinction: The NICHD/ACOG Category I–III framework is not identical to the NICE or FIGO classification systems. Some examinations expect a guideline-specific classification. Learn the system prescribed by your institution and avoid mixing its definitions with another system.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. How to report a CTG in the examination

blocks.text: Use a structured statement:

“ This CTG was performed for [indication] at [gestational age]. The trace quality is [adequate/limited]. The baseline fetal heart rate is approximately [value] bpm, with [normal/reduced/increased] variability. Accelerations are [present/absent]. Decelerations are [absent/present, with type and pattern]. Uterine activity is approximately [number] contractions per 10 minutes, lasting [duration]. Overall, the CTG is classified as [classification under the specified guideline]. My management plan is to [actions], with [level of urgency] senior review and reassessment.”
Avoid reporting only “CTG is abnormal.” Describe the actual features and explain what you will do.
Q1. What is the normal baseline fetal heart rate?
Usually 110–160 bpm during labour.
Q2. What does normal variability indicate?
It is generally reassuring regarding fetal autonomic activity and oxygenation when interpreted alongside the full trace and clinical context.
Q3. Are accelerations required for a normal intrapartum CTG?
No. Their absence alone does not establish fetal hypoxia.
Q4. What is the likely mechanism of late decelerations?
They are associated with impaired uteroplacental oxygen transfer, although the clinical context and other CTG features determine significance.
Q5. What is the first action if there is a sudden sustained fetal heart rate drop?
Call for urgent help, assess the mother and trace, identify reversible causes such as cord prolapse or maternal hypotension, and prepare for expedited delivery if necessary.
Q6. Should you give oxygen to every woman with an abnormal CTG?
No. Oxygen is indicated for maternal hypoxaemia or another appropriate maternal indication, not routinely for an abnormal CTG when maternal oxygenation is normal.
Q7. Why must you assess contractions?
Excessive uterine activity can compromise fetal oxygen transfer and may require modification of oxytocin or other treatment.
Q8. Can CTG alone diagnose fetal acidosis?
No. CTG provides an assessment of fetal heart rate patterns and risk. It cannot directly establish fetal acid–base status in every case.
